a: the LORD answered Job
p: For 35 chapters the speakers say "God" or "the Almighty". Now the narrator's name for God, the LORD, returns.
b: In the poetry the speakers almost never use the name YHWH ("the LORD"); they say El, Eloah, Elohim or Shaddai, as non-Israelites from the East might. The name comes back here, as in the prose frame (chapters 1–2 and 42:7–17). It tells the reader that the God of Israel himself now speaks, the one who allowed the test in chapter 1. He answers Job, not the friends and not Elihu, who has just finished (37:24). Job had begged for an answer (13:22; 31:35). He gets one, but not the one he asked for: God never mentions the wager with the Accuser.

a: from the windstorm
p: The storm is the setting of theophany: Sinai, Elijah, the psalms. Elihu has just described one coming (37).
b: Se'arah is a violent windstorm. God appears in storms at Sinai, where "there was thunder and flashes of lightning, a heavy cloud on the mountain" (Exodus 19:16), and Elijah is carried off "in the windstorm" (2 Kings 2:11), the same word. Elihu's last speech described a gathering thunderstorm (36:27–37:22), so the reader may feel the storm arriving as he speaks. Job had said that God "bruises me in a windstorm" (9:17, the same word with a different spelling). Now the storm brings not crushing but speech. Ezekiel's vision also begins with a storm wind out of the north (Ezekiel 1:4).

a: Who is this who blurs the plan
p: 'Etsah is a plan, design or purpose. God does not say Job is wicked; he says Job talks without knowing the plan.
b: Machshikh 'etsah is literally "making the plan dark". 'Etsah can mean advice, but here it is God's design for the world, the order he is about to show. The charge is ignorance, not sin. God never takes up the friends' claim that Job is being punished for wrongdoing. Job will quote this line back in 42:3, with a different verb ("hides"). Many readers hear a reproof of Job; others (Habel, Newsom) note that God's rebuke is also an invitation: Job has spoken about a world he has not yet seen.

a: Get your belt tight, like a man
p: Literally "gird your loins": tuck your robe into your belt, to fight or run. God accepts Job's challenge.
b: The Hebrew says "gird your loins like a gever", a strong man or warrior. A man in a long robe tucked it into his belt before running or fighting (1 Kings 18:46). God takes up the legal challenge Job laid down (13:22; 31:35–37) and turns it around: Job wanted to question God; now God will question him. "You tell me what you know" is literally "make me know", the language of a witness giving testimony. The same summons opens the second speech (40:7) and Job quotes it at 42:4.

a: Where were you when I founded the earth?
p: Verses 4–7 picture creation as a builder setting a house on its foundations, with measuring line and cornerstone.
b: God speaks of the earth as a building: founding it, measuring it, stretching a line, sinking its bases and setting the corner stone, with a celebration when the stone is laid (verse 7). Ancient temple builders held such ceremonies, and Ezra 3:10–11 describes singing when the foundation of the second Temple was laid. The point of the question is not geology. Job was not there when the order of the world was set, and so he cannot judge it. Proverbs uses the same picture of Wisdom present at creation (Proverbs 8:27–30).

a: the stars of morning sang as one
t: Morning stars and sons of God
p: The stars and the heavenly beings sing at creation. The Greek reads "all my angels".
b: The "sons of God" are the heavenly beings of 1:6 and 2:1 (see the note there). Here they cheer the founding of the earth, so they existed before it. The stars are paired with them, as heavenly beings are elsewhere (Judges 5:20 says "The stars fought from heaven"). The Greek translation has "all my angels praised me with a great voice". Jewish and Christian readers drew from this verse that the angels were made before the world (Augustine discusses it, City of God 11.9). Revelation calls Jesus "the bright morning star" (Revelation 22:16), a different use of the image.

a: Who closed doors to hold back the sea
p: In other ancient myths the sea is an enemy god. Here it is a baby God dresses and puts to bed.
b: In the Babylonian Enuma Elish the storm god Marduk kills Tiamat, the salt sea, and builds the world from her body. In the Ugaritic Baal myths Baal fights Yam, "Sea". The Bible knows this picture: God "crushed Rahab" and broke the sea monsters (Psalm 89:10; Psalm 74:13). Job himself has used it (7:12; 9:13; 26:12). But here the sea is not a defeated enemy. It bursts from the womb, and God wraps it in clouds like a newborn and sets limits for it, a parent with a strong child. Most scholars see a deliberate reworking of the myth: the chaos is real, but it is God's creature.

a: Here a stop is set for your proud waves
p: God's limit for the sea is a common theme: Genesis 1, Proverbs 8, Psalm 104, Jeremiah 5.
b: In Genesis God says, "Let the waters under the sky be gathered to one place, and let dry ground be seen" (Genesis 1:9). Proverbs 8:29 has God setting the sea its limit so that the waters would not pass his command, and Psalm 104:9 says he set a boundary they cannot cross. Jeremiah 5:22 makes it an argument: God set the sand as a boundary for the sea, and its waves roar but cannot pass, so why does his people not fear him? In Job the boundary is a sign of care as well as power. The sea is allowed its pride, but only so far.

a: the wicked are shaken loose from it
p: The dawn grabs the earth like a blanket by its corners and shakes off the night's evildoers.
b: The "corners" (kanfot, literally "wings") are the edges of a garment or blanket. Each morning the light seizes the earth by its edges and shakes out the wicked, who work at night (24:13–17). God does not destroy the wicked here; he limits them by the daily coming of light. The verse quietly answers Job's complaint that God lets the wicked run free (24:1–12): there is a check on them built into the order of each day, even if it is not the full justice Job wants. In the Hebrew text the letter ayin in "wicked" (resha'im) is written raised above the line here and in verse 15; the reason is unknown.

a: The earth changes like clay under a seal
t: A hard verse: clay and clothing
p: As a seal stamps a picture into soft clay, dawn makes the earth's shapes appear. The second line is unclear.
b: A cylinder seal rolled over wet clay brings out a raised picture. At dawn the shapeless dark earth takes on hills, trees and buildings, as if stamped. The second line, literally "they stand forth like clothing", is less clear. Many take it as the earth's features standing out like the folds or colors of a garment. Others change one letter to read "it is dyed like a garment" (Dhorme, Pope, and many modern versions). The Greek has something quite different: "Did you take clay from the earth and form a living being, and set it on the earth able to speak?"

a: The wicked lose their light
p: For the wicked, darkness is their "light", their working hours. Dawn takes it away from them.
b: The wicked's "light" is probably the night, the time they love (24:17: "Morning, for every one of them, is deep darkness"). Dawn takes it away. "The arm they lift high" is the arm raised to strike, which is broken. This is the first of several places where God's speeches touch justice. They do not deny that there are wicked people; they show a God who limits them within the order of the world.

a: the gates of deep shadow
p: Tsalmavet, traditionally "the shadow of death", is the deepest darkness, here the darkness of the world of the dead.
b: Tsalmavet was read in ancient times as tsel mavet, "shadow of death" (so the Greek and KJV, and famously Psalm 23:4). Many scholars think it is one word, "deep darkness", from a root meaning dark. Here it stands beside "death" as a name for the underworld, which was pictured as a city with gates (Isaiah 38:10; Psalm 9:13; Matthew 16:18). Job had longed for that land of darkness (10:21–22). God asks whether he has even seen its gates. The rendering "deep shadow" matches the rest of Job on this site (3:5).

a: Of course you know: you were born by then!
p: God mocks gently: Job must be very old, if he was there when light was given its home.
b: The verse is sarcasm, as most translations show. It echoes Eliphaz's taunt, "Was it you, born the first of humankind?" (15:7). Some readers find God's irony harsh to a man in grief. Others hear humor: God speaks to Job as one adult to another, not as a judge to a criminal. Either way, the questions are not a demand for answers but a way to make Job feel the size of the world.

a: the places where snow is stored
p: Ancient people pictured the sky with storerooms for snow, hail, wind and rain, opened when God chose.
b: The "storehouses" (otsrot) of snow and hail belong to the ancient picture of the sky as a great building with rooms for the weather (Deuteronomy 28:12; Psalm 135:7; Jeremiah 10:13). Hail as a weapon "for a day of fighting and war" recalls the hailstorm of the plagues (Exodus 9:22–26) and the hailstones that killed the Amorites at Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11). God keeps the weather for his own purposes, and Job cannot even reach the doors.

a: to send rain on ground with nobody on it
p: God waters the desert, where no human will benefit. The world is not built around people.
b: This is one of the most important lines in the speeches. Job and his friends all assumed that God's actions are about humans: reward or punishment. God describes rain falling where no one lives, simply to make the desert bloom. Many interpreters (Habel, Newsom, Alter) see here the heart of the answer: creation has purposes of its own, and humans are not the measure of everything. Others (Andersen, Hartley) stress that the same care shown to the empty desert is shown to Job. The two readings can stand together.

a: Is there a father for the rain?
p: Canaanite religion gave the rain a divine father or lord. Here rain and ice have no divine parents.
b: In Ugaritic texts Baal is the lord of rain and dew, and his daughters include Tallay, "Dewy", and Pidray, perhaps "Misty". The questions "Is there a father for the rain?" and "Whose womb does the ice come out of?" may be aimed at such ideas: there is no family of weather gods. Or they may simply be poetic: the answer is that God alone is the source, both father and mother of the weather (compare the womb of the sea in verse 8). Either way, the verse is often noted for giving God both a father's and a mother's role.

a: Can you tie the knots that hold the Pleiades
p: Kimah and Kesil are probably the Pleiades and Orion. The Bear may be the Big Dipper. All are uncertain.
b: Job named the same stars in 9:9, and Amos 5:8 calls God the maker of Kimah and Kesil. Kimah (perhaps "heap") is usually the Pleiades, the tight star cluster. Kesil means "fool" and is usually Orion, perhaps pictured as a giant bound in the sky; the Targum calls him the "giant". "The Bear and her young" ('Ayish) may be the Big Dipper and its tail, or Aldebaran and the Hyades. The KJV's "sweet influences of Pleiades" reads ma'adannot as "delights" instead of "bonds". God asks whether Job can lead the seasons of the stars, which mark the farmer's year.

a: the star-groups
p: Mazzaroth is a mystery word, perhaps the constellations of the zodiac. The Greek simply copies it.
b: Mazzarot appears only here. It may be the same as mazzalot in 2 Kings 23:5, the constellations (or the zodiac signs) that Josiah stopped people worshiping, and later Hebrew mazzal, "constellation, luck" (as in mazal tov). The Greek translator did not know it and copied it as mazouroth; the Vulgate has "Lucifer", the morning star. "Star-groups" is the most likely sense.

a: Who has put wisdom in what lies hidden?
t: Hidden parts, or ibis and rooster?
p: Two rare words: "inner parts" and "mind", or two weather-wise birds, the ibis and the rooster.
b: Tuchot appears elsewhere only in Psalm 51:6, "inward parts". Sekhvi appears only here. The traditional reading is "wisdom in the inner parts... understanding to the mind" (KJV). But the verse sits among weather questions, and an old Jewish tradition says sekhvi means "rooster" (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 26a); the morning blessing thanks God "who gave the rooster understanding to tell day from night" (Berakhot 60b), and the Vulgate also has "rooster". Many modern scholars then take tuchot as the ibis, the bird of the Egyptian god Thoth, thought to foretell the Nile flood. Others suggest "clouds" and "sky phenomena". The Greek has "Who gave women skill at weaving?" The Plain keeps the general sense; the bird reading is a strong alternative.

a: the sky's waterskins
p: Clouds are pictured as leather water bags that God tips over to pour rain.
b: A waterskin was a goat hide sewn into a bag. God tips the bags of the sky (literally "makes them lie down") so that the dry soil, cracked into clods, runs together into mud (verse 38). Job had used the same picture: God binds up the waters in his clouds (26:8).

a: Will you track down food for the lion
t: Wild animals: God's care for predators
p: The tour now turns to animals, most of them wild, many of them hunters. God feeds even the lion and the raven.
b: From here to 39:30 God names ten creatures: lion, raven, ibex, deer, wild donkey, wild ox, ostrich, horse, hawk and eagle. All but the horse live beyond human control. Several are predators, and the passage ends with eagle chicks drinking blood (39:30). God does not hide the violence of nature; he claims it. Readers take this differently. For some it shows God's care reaching even the hunter and the hungry chick (Psalm 104:21; Psalm 147:9). For others it shows a world that is not tidy or moral in human terms, but is still God's and still good to him (Newsom, Alter).

a: Who has the raven's meal ready
p: The raven was unclean and noisy, yet God hears its chicks. Jesus uses the same picture in Luke 12:24.
b: The raven was an unclean bird (Leviticus 11:15), and folklore said it neglected its young. Yet its chicks "call to God". Psalm 147:9 praises God who gives the animals food, and to the young ravens that call out. Jesus tells his hearers to look at the ravens, which neither plant nor harvest and have no barn, and yet God feeds them (Luke 12:24; Matthew 6:26 has "birds"). Ravens also fed Elijah (1 Kings 17:4–6). In Job the point is first about God's knowledge and care for the wild, and only by implication about Job.

a: the ibex of the crags
p: Ya'alei sela', "goats of the rock", are the Nubian ibex, which still live on the cliffs at En-gedi.
b: The Nubian ibex lives in the cliffs of the Judean desert and the Negev; David hid from Saul near "the Ibex Rocks" at En-gedi (1 Samuel 24:2). Ibex give birth in remote places, unseen by people. God asks whether Job knows the time of their calving and watches over it, as a shepherd would for his own flock. No human tends these animals, but God does. The "deer" (ayyalot) are does, probably fallow or red deer, now gone from the region.

a: they never return to their mothers
p: Wild young grow up and go, never coming back. For a father who lost all his children, a striking image.
b: The young of wild animals grow strong "out in the wild" and leave for good. Some readers find the line painful in a book that began with the death of Job's ten children (1:18–19). Others see a lesson: in God's world life moves on, and parents, human or animal, do not own their young. The text itself makes no comment.

a: the wild donkey
p: The wild donkey stands for freedom from all human control: no town, no driver, no load.
b: Two words are used: pere', the wild donkey, and 'arod, probably the onager or Asian wild ass. Both are free animals that no one rides. The angel said Ishmael would be "a wild donkey of a man" (Genesis 16:12, same word pere'), and Job himself had compared the poor to wild donkeys scrounging in the desert (24:5). Here God speaks of the animal's freedom as his own gift: he "set it loose" and gave it the desert as its home. The donkey "laughs" at the town, the first of several creatures that laugh at humans (39:18, 22; 41:29).

a: the wild ox
p: Re'em is the wild ox or aurochs. The Greek "monokeros", one-horned, gave the KJV its "unicorn".
b: Re'em is the aurochs, a huge wild bull, now extinct, known in Akkadian as rimu and hunted by Assyrian kings. It was famous for its horns (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 92:10). The Greek translators rendered it monokeros, "one-horned", perhaps because animals in side view show one horn, and the Latin unicornis led to the KJV "unicorn". The real point is that this is the wild cousin of the farmer's ox. It will never pull a plow or bring in a harvest (verses 10–12).

a: The ostrich flaps its wings with delight
t: The ostrich passage and the stork
p: A riddle-line full of rare words. The "stork" (chasidah) also sounds like "kind, loyal": the ostrich is not.
b: "Ostrich" is renanim, perhaps "screechers". The second line is literally "if a pinion, stork (chasidah) and plumage". Chasidah means stork but sounds like chasid, "loyal, kind" (from hesed, "loyal love"). So the line may hint: the ostrich has wings, but they are not the wings of the stork, the bird famous for care of its young. Lamentations 4:3 also calls the ostrich cruel. In fact ostriches guard their nests carefully, but ancient people saw eggs left in the sand by day and drew their own conclusions. The Old Greek translation lacked 39:13–18; the Greek copies we have fill the gap from Theodotion, and Rahlfs marks the lines with asterisks.

a: God has let wisdom slip from its mind
t: A foolish creature, made by God
p: God made a bird without sense, and says so with a smile. Not everything in creation is wise or useful.
b: Here God speaks of himself in the third person ("Eloah has made it forget wisdom"), as also in 38:41 and 40:19. Some critics take the ostrich passage as a later addition, partly because the Old Greek lacked it (see 39:13); others see a deliberate change of voice. The theology is striking: God made a creature without wisdom, which mistreats its young, and yet it can outrun a horse (verse 18). The world includes the absurd and the comic. Gregory the Great read the ostrich as a picture of hypocrites, who show the feathers of holiness but cannot fly. Modern readers usually take it as a sign that God enjoys a world that is not built on human rules.

a: who dresses its neck in a rippling mane
p: Ra'mah is related to ra'am, "thunder". The KJV says "clothed his neck with thunder". Most now read "mane".
b: The word ra'mah comes from a root "to tremble, thunder" (as in ra'am, thunder). The KJV has "Hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?", a memorable line. Most modern scholars think the word means the mane, which quivers or ripples as the horse moves, though some keep a sense of terror or power (the Greek has "fear"). The war horse is the only domestic animal in the list, but it is pictured at its wildest, in battle.

a: At the blast of the ram's horn it will not hold still
p: Literally "it does not stand firm" or "it does not believe": the horse cannot believe its luck, or cannot keep still.
b: Lo ya'amin usually means "it does not believe" (from the root of "amen"). The KJV takes it so: "neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet". Many scholars take the verb in an older sense, "stand firm, stay still" (compare Isaiah 7:9, a wordplay on the same root). The horse is so eager for battle that it cannot stay in place when the ram's horn sounds. The horn is the shofar, used for signals in war (Judges 7:18–20).

a: wherever there are bodies, it is there
p: Jesus' saying about vultures gathering where the corpse is (Matthew 24:28) echoes this line.
b: Nesher, translated "eagle", also covers the griffon vulture, and here the bird gathers at the slain after battle. Jesus' saying that wherever a dead body lies, the vultures flock to it (Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37) uses the same picture and may echo this verse. The speech that began with stars singing at creation (38:7) ends with chicks drinking blood. God does not apologize for either.

a: Is the critic going to take the Almighty to court?
p: The verb rib means to bring a lawsuit. God sums up Job's case as a lawsuit against the Almighty.
b: Rov (from riv) is the language of the law court: Job wanted to bring a case against God (9:3; 13:3; 23:4–7). "Critic" (yissor) is a fault-finder or corrector, a rare form. "The Almighty" is Shaddai and "God" is Eloah, the divine names used throughout the poetry (see the notes at their first use earlier in the book). The first speech ends with an invitation, not a sentence: answer, if you will.

a: I am a lightweight
p: Qalloti, "I am light": the opposite of kavod, "heavy, weighty, glorious". Not "vile", as in the KJV.
b: The KJV's "I am vile" is too strong. Qal means light, of little weight or account. In Hebrew, honor and glory (kavod) are "heaviness", so Job says he has no weight to throw around before God. It is not a confession of sin. Putting a hand over the mouth means silence out of respect: the princes did it when Job spoke in his better days (29:9), and Job had told the friends to do it (21:5). Now he does it himself. But he does not yet withdraw his case: "I will not reply... I will not go on" (verse 5). Most readers see this as a pause, which is why God speaks again.

a: One time I talked, and I will not reply
p: A Hebrew way of saying "more than enough" (compare Psalm 62:11; Proverbs 30:15–31).
b: The pattern "one... two" (and in Proverbs "three... four") is a poetic way to say "I have said it, and said it again". Job does not say he was wrong. He says he has nothing more to add. Some readers (Andersen, Hartley) hear humility; others (Curtis, Clines in part) hear a dignified or even sullen silence. The second speech suggests God wanted more than silence.

a: Would you even overturn my justice?
t: The central question of the second speech
p: God names the danger in Job's case: to be right himself, Job has had to make God wrong.
b: Mishpat is justice, but also God's right ordering of the world. Job had insisted on his innocence and so concluded that God was unjust (9:22–24; 19:6; 27:2). God's question is the turning point of the speeches. He does not say Job is guilty; he asks whether Job must declare God guilty in order to be innocent himself. Elihu had made a similar charge (32:2; 34:5–6). Newsom and others see here the core of God's answer: both can be true at once, that Job is innocent and that God is not unjust, but Job has made it a contest in which one must lose.

a: put on pride and loftiness as jewelry
p: God dares Job to put on the royal robes of the divine king and do the work of bringing down the proud.
b: The four words (ga'on, gova, hod, hadar) are royal and divine: Psalm 104:1 says God is clothed in splendor and majesty (hod vehadar), and Psalm 93:1 that the LORD reigns, robed in majesty. God invites Job to play king for a day. If Job can humble every proud person and bury the wicked (verses 11–13), then God himself will "give him credit" (verse 14), a word (odekka) used elsewhere for praising God. The irony is plain, but some readers also hear a serious point: ruling the world justly is harder than Job imagines.

a: bind their faces in the hidden place below
p: Tamun, "the hidden place", is the grave or the underworld, where the faces of the dead are wrapped.
b: Tamun means hidden or buried. Here it is the world of the dead, Sheol. Binding the faces may refer to wrapping the dead (John 11:44) or to the darkness of the underworld. If Job could send every wicked person to the grave at once, then he could claim to save himself (verse 14).

a: Behemoth
p: Hippopotamus, elephant, mythic monster, or a real animal drawn larger than life. Each view has strong support.
b: Behemot is the plural of behemah, "beast" (often "cattle"), used as a singular: "the Beast of beasts". The verbs are singular, so it is one creature. (1) A real animal. Since Samuel Bochart (1663) most have said the hippopotamus: it eats grass, lies among reeds and lotus, and is not alarmed by a flooding river. Aquinas and Calvin, following older tradition, said the elephant. (2) A mythic beast. John Day, Marvin Pope and others connect it with a bull-like monster that Anat claims to have killed at Ugarit, "El's calf", and note that Jewish tradition pairs it with Leviathan as the two great monsters (see 40:19). (3) Both. Othmar Keel and others argue the poet drew a real hippo, but with the mythic weight it had in Egypt, where the king hunting the hippo stood for Horus defeating chaos (Seth). (4) Some young-earth creationists (Henry Morris and others) read it as a sauropod dinosaur, because of the tail like a cedar (verse 17); most scholars reject this.

a: which I made as well as you
p: "Which I made with you": Behemoth is Job's fellow creature, made by the same God.
b: The Hebrew is literally "which I made with you". Whatever Behemoth is, God made it, as he made Job. It is not a rival god. Many readers see this as the key to both beasts: the most fearsome powers in the world, whether animals or symbols of chaos, are creatures under God's hand. The Greek has the plural, "beasts are with you".

a: Its tail stands rigid like a cedar
p: A hippo's tail is short. So "tail" may be a polite word for the male organ, as the Latin "testicles" in the next line suggests.
b: A cedar-like tail does not fit a hippopotamus or elephant, whose tails are small. Many scholars think "tail" is a euphemism for the male member, pointing to Behemoth's sexual power, and that "thighs" (pachadav) in the second line means the testicles. The Vulgate reads it so ("the sinews of his testicles are woven together"). Others (Hartley) keep "tail" and see the poet exaggerating: the hippo's stubby tail swings with the strength of a tree. Readers who see a dinosaur cite this verse.

a: It is the first of the ways of God
p: The same words describe Wisdom in Proverbs 8:22. Behemoth is a masterpiece, perhaps the first creature made.
b: Reshit darkhe El, "the first of the ways of God", recalls Proverbs 8:22, where Wisdom says, "The LORD made me the beginning of his way, the first of his works long ago". "First" may mean first in time (made at the start) or first in rank (the greatest). Jewish and Christian readers both took it as a sign that Behemoth was more than an animal. Gregory the Great read it as the devil, the first and greatest angel before his fall. The second line is unclear. Literally it says "the one who made it, let him bring near his sword", which the Plain keeps. It may mean that only God can come at it with a sword, or that God gave it a sword (its tusks). The Greek reads "made to be mocked by his angels" (see the variant).

a: The hills carry their crops to it
p: Jewish tradition linked Behemoth with "the animals (behemot) on a thousand hills" in Psalm 50:10.
b: Psalm 50:10 says the animals "on a thousand hills" belong to God, using the word behemot. Later rabbis read it as Behemoth itself, a giant beast that eats the grass of a thousand hills each day (Leviticus Rabbah 22:10). The poet's picture is simpler: the hills give it food, and the other animals play near it without fear. Behemoth eats grass (verse 15); it is not a predator.

a: the thorny lotus bushes
p: Tse'elim is probably the thorny lotus bush (Ziziphus lotus) that grows by water in the Jordan valley, not the water lily.
b: The word tse'elim appears only here and in verse 22. It is usually identified as Ziziphus lotus, a thorny shrub that grows in hot, wet places such as the Jordan valley, not the Egyptian water lily. With reeds, swamp and poplars (or willows) of the wadi, it gives a river-marsh home. That fits the hippopotamus, and hippo bones from ancient times have been reported along the coastal rivers of Israel.

a: the Jordan
p: Hippos did not live in the Jordan in Bible times. "Jordan" may be used for any great river, or for the poet's own landscape.
b: Hippopotamuses lived in the Nile and, in earlier ages, in the rivers of the Levant, but there is no clear evidence of them in the Jordan in Israel's time. Some scholars think "Jordan" here means any rushing river (Dhorme, Gordis), others that the poet is using the most famous river his readers knew, or that Behemoth is no ordinary animal. Some delete "Jordan" as a gloss. The point is the beast's calm: a flood "bursts against its mouth" and it does not care.

a: Will someone catch it with its eyes wide open?
p: Be'enav, "in its eyes", may mean "while it watches", or hooks through the eyes. The line may have lost a word.
b: The Hebrew is literally "in (or by) its eyes, will one take it?" The Plain takes it as "in full view": no one can catch it while it is watching. Others read "by its eyes", that is, with hooks or rings through the eyes, matching "through the nose" in the second line. The line is short, and some scholars think a word such as "who" has dropped out at the start ("Who can take it by its eyes?"). The sense in every case is that Behemoth cannot be captured.

a: Will you haul Leviathan up on a fishhook?
p: English 41:1–8 is Hebrew 40:25–32, and English 41:9–34 is Hebrew 41:1–26. The Latin Vulgate numbers differently again.
b: Printed Hebrew Bibles, and Jewish translations such as the JPS, run chapter 40 on to verse 32, so the Leviathan poem begins at Hebrew 40:25. English 41:1–8 is Hebrew 40:25–32, and English 41:9–34 is Hebrew 41:1–26. The Greek (Rahlfs) and modern Jewish Bibles follow the Hebrew numbers. The older Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims number differently again: English 40:1–5 is their 39:31–35, Behemoth begins at their 40:10, Leviathan at their 40:20, and English 41:10–34 is their 41:1–25. This site uses the English numbers, so a Jewish commentary's "Job 41:1" is English 41:9, and a Latin writer's "Job 41:24" is English 41:33. No words are added or missing; only the chapter breaks move. (The chapter divisions are medieval and were added to the Hebrew text later.)

a: Leviathan
p: Crocodile, whale, or the chaos dragon of the sea. Many readers think the poet means a real animal and a myth at once.
b: Livyatan probably means "the coiling one". (1) A real animal. Since Bochart (1663), many have identified it with the Nile crocodile: armored hide, terrible teeth, eyes that rise above the water at dawn, hunted with hooks and harpoons in Egypt. Older Christian writers often said the whale (Aquinas, Calvin). (2) The chaos monster. In Ugaritic myth Baal (or Anat) defeats Lotan, the twisting serpent with seven heads, and the Bible uses the same name and phrases: Isaiah 27:1, Psalm 74:14, and Job 3:8 ("those who are ready to wake Leviathan"). Fire-breathing (41:18–21) and the fear of the gods (41:25) suit a dragon more than a reptile. (3) Both. Many scholars (Keel, Habel, Newsom) think the poet describes a crocodile in mythic colors. The striking thing is that Leviathan, which God crushed in Psalm 74, here is a creature God made and admires; in Psalm 104:26 God formed it to play.

a: Will you tie its tongue down with a line?
p: Egyptians hunted crocodiles and hippos with hooks, ropes and harpoons. God asks whether Job could do it alone.
b: The Greek historian Herodotus (2.70) describes Egyptians catching crocodiles with a baited hook and a pig's back, then pulling them ashore and plastering their eyes with mud. Egyptian tomb reliefs show hunters harpooning hippopotamuses from papyrus boats, and the king's hunt stood for the triumph of order over chaos. The questions in verses 1–8 run through the stages of a hunt and then mock it: Leviathan will not beg for mercy, become a pet, or be sold in pieces at market.

a: Will it make a treaty with you
p: Berit is a covenant; "slave for good" is the legal phrase for a servant who chooses to stay for life (Exodus 21:6).
b: God imagines Leviathan negotiating a berit, a covenant or treaty, and becoming an 'eved 'olam, a "slave for good", the term the law uses for a servant who chooses to stay with his master for life: his master is to pierce his ear, "Then he will serve him for life" (Exodus 21:6; Deuteronomy 15:17). The joke is that the great beast will never agree to such terms. Some see a deeper echo: God made a covenant with Noah that included the animals (Genesis 9:9–10). Humans cannot.
orig: הֲיִכְרֹת בְּרִית... לְעֶבֶד עוֹלָם (hayikhrot berit... le'eved 'olam)

a: split it up among the dealers
p: The word for "dealers" is kena'anim, "Canaanites": the Phoenicians were the merchants of the ancient world.
b: In several places kena'ani, "Canaanite", simply means "merchant" (Proverbs 31:24; Zephaniah 1:11; Hosea 12:7), because the Phoenicians of the coast were famous traders. "Partners in trade" (chabbarim) were members of a merchants' company. The rabbis read the same word as "companions", meaning scholars, and found here the feast of the righteous on Leviathan's flesh (Bava Batra 75a; see 41:7).

a: Will you stuff its skin full of barbs
p: Jewish tradition says Leviathan will be served to the righteous at the end of days, and its skin made into a booth.
b: Rabbinic teaching built on these verses. The Talmud (Bava Batra 74b–75a) says God made Leviathan male and female, killed the female and salted her away for the righteous in the world to come; that the angel Gabriel will one day hunt Leviathan, quoting 41:1; that the companions of 41:6 are scholars who will feast on it; and that from its skin God will make booths for them, reading sukkot, the word for "barbs" in this verse, as "booths". Earlier, 1 Enoch 60:7–9, 4 Ezra 6:49–52 and 2 Baruch 29:4 describe Behemoth and Leviathan kept for the last days as food. Many Jews still say, on leaving the sukkah at the end of the Festival of Booths, a prayer to be worthy to sit in the sukkah made of Leviathan's skin.

a: One glimpse of it, and he is thrown down
p: "His hope" is the hope of anyone who tries. Many read the second line "even a god is thrown down at the sight of it".
b: The Hebrew says "his hope is a lie". The "he" is anyone who tries the hunt just described. In the second line, hagam 'el mar'av yutal, the small word 'el can be the preposition "at" ("at the sight of it he is thrown down"), which the Plain follows, or the noun "god": "even a god is thrown down at the sight of it" (Pope, Habel and others). That fits 41:25, where the gods fear Leviathan. Verse 9 begins chapter 41 in the Hebrew numbering (Hebrew 41:1).
orig: תֹחַלְתּוֹ נִכְזָבָה; הֲגַם אֶל־מַרְאָיו יֻטָל (tochalto nikhzavah; hagam 'el-mar'av yutal)

a: So who is he who would take a stand against me?
p: The point of the whole Leviathan poem in one line: if no one dares wake the beast, who can stand against its Maker?
b: Verses 10–11 step out from the description to speak of God himself. If no human dares stir up Leviathan, how could anyone stand against the God who made it and plays with it? This connects the poem to Job's lawsuit (40:2, 8). For the reading "before him", which keeps both lines on the beast, see the variant.

a: Who has ever faced me and then made me repay him?
p: Paul quotes this line in Romans 11:35: no one has given to God first so that God owes him.
b: Paul closes his long argument about Israel and the nations with a hymn: "Who has given to him first, so that he must be paid back?" (Romans 11:35). His wording follows the Hebrew of this verse more closely than the Greek translation, which has "Who will stand against me and endure?" For Paul it means that God's gifts are grace; no one can put God in debt. In Job it answers Job's demand that God owes him a hearing. "Faced me" (hiqdimani) can also mean "came before me", "gave to me first".

a: I will not keep quiet about its limbs
p: Baddav may be "its limbs" or "its boasts" (as in 11:3, "your bragging").
b: Bad can mean a limb or part (18:13) or empty talk (11:3, "your bragging"). If "limbs", God announces a full description of the beast's body, which follows. If "boasts", God refuses to put up with Leviathan's (or Job's) big talk. The Plain takes "limbs" because the next verses describe the body. For the Ketiv and Qere at the start of the verse, see the variant.

a: Who could get between its double jaws?
p: The Hebrew says "the double of its bridle", probably the two jaws where a bridle would go.
b: Kefel risno is literally "the doubling of its bridle (halter)". Most take it as the jaws, the place where a bit or bridle sits. Some read siryono, "its coat of mail", with the Greek, and translate "its double armor". The first line, "the face of its clothing", is its outer skin or armor.

a: Its pride is its rows of shields
p: Ga'avah means "pride". With a change of vowels it becomes gevo, "its back", as the Vulgate seems to read.
b: The Hebrew has ga'avah, "pride": the beast's glory is its armor of scales, set like rows of shields. Many scholars read gevo, "its back", by a change of vowels only (the Vulgate has "its body"). Both fit: crocodile scales on the back look like rows of shields. The Plain keeps the Hebrew. Pride returns in verse 34, where Leviathan is king of the proud.

a: its eyes are like the eyelids of dawn
p: In Egyptian writing, the crocodile's eyes stood for sunrise. The phrase "eyelids of dawn" also appears in 3:9.
b: A Greek book on Egyptian hieroglyphs, the Hieroglyphica of Horapollo (1.68), says that to write "sunrise" the Egyptians drew a crocodile's eyes, because they appear first when the animal surfaces. That is a striking match for this line, and Bochart used it to argue for the crocodile. Job used "the eyelids of dawn" in his curse on his birthday (3:9), the same speech in which he called on those "ready to wake Leviathan" (3:8). The sneezing that flashes light may describe spray glittering in the sun.

a: Torches shoot from its mouth
p: No crocodile breathes fire. Verses 18–21 describe a dragon, whether as poetry or as myth.
b: Smoke, flame and coals from the mouth belong to the dragon of myth, and in the Bible to God himself in the storm (Psalm 18:8: smoke went up from his nostrils and fire from his mouth). Those who read Leviathan as a crocodile take these lines as poetic exaggeration, like steamy breath on a cold morning. Those who read it as the chaos monster take them literally within the myth. Either way, the poet makes Leviathan godlike, and then says God made it.

a: the gods are afraid
p: 'Elim can mean "gods" (Exodus 15:11) or "mighty ones". Most modern scholars read "gods".
b: 'Elim is the plural of 'el, "god". In Exodus 15:11 it plainly means gods ("Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?"). Here many scholars (Pope, Habel, Clines) take it so: even the heavenly beings fear Leviathan, as the gods feared Tiamat in the Babylonian myth. Jewish tradition and many translations read "the mighty", strong men (Rashi; KJV). The second line is literally "from crashings they miss the way" or "they purify themselves" (KJV); "they lose their wits" is the most likely sense.

a: It brings the deep to a boil
p: The beast stirs the deep (tehom) like a pot. The Greek even names Tartarus, the deepest pit.
b: Tehom, "the deep", is the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2 ("Darkness lay on the face of the deep"). Leviathan churns it like boiling water or a perfume-maker's pot of ointment, and leaves a white wake that looks like an old man's gray hair (verse 32). The Greek of verse 32 adds that it holds "the Tartarus of the abyss as a captive". In the Bible the sea and its monster are God's to command: "There the ships go, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it" (a fresh rendering of Psalm 104:26).

a: it is king of all the proud creatures
p: Thomas Hobbes named the all-powerful state Leviathan (1651) after this verse. Gregory read it as the devil.
b: The phrase bene shachats, "sons of pride", appears also in 28:8, where it means proud wild beasts, so the Plain says "proud creatures". The Greek has "king of all that are in the waters". The second speech had told Job to humble every proud one (40:11–12) if he could; here is a creature only God can humble. Gregory the Great read the verse as the devil, king of all the proud. Thomas Hobbes named his book on the absolute state Leviathan (1651), and its title page quotes the Latin of verse 33 (Vulgate 41:24): there is no power on earth to be compared with him.

a: I know there is nothing you cannot do
p: Job confesses God's power and freedom, not (yet) his justice. For the Ketiv "you know", see the variant.
b: Job says that God can do anything and that nothing he intends can be stopped. He does not say that God is just; he says that God is free and able. Some readers find this a full surrender, others a careful statement that leaves his case open. For the written form "you know" and the Masoretic reading "I know", see the variant.

a: 'Who is this who hides the plan without knowing anything?'
p: Verse 3a repeats God's words in 38:2, and 4b repeats 38:3. God never says 4a; the quotation marks there are an interpretation.
b: Job quotes God's opening challenge (38:2) in 3a and his summons (38:3; 40:7) in 4b, and answers each. The Hebrew has no "You asked" or "You said"; many translations add such words, and the Plain uses quotation marks instead. God never says the words of 4a ("Hear me, please, and I will do the talking"). The Plain's quotation marks make it part of Job's paraphrase of God's summons; others take 4a as Job recalling his own earlier challenge (13:22), and some scholars take 3a and 4 as later notes copied in. Either way, Job admits he spoke of "wonders beyond me" (nifla'ot, the word for God's wonders in Exodus 3:20 and Psalm 136:4). His answer concerns his knowledge, not his guilt.

a: but now my own eye has seen you
p: Job has met God. Many readers see here the real answer of the book: not an explanation but a presence.
b: Job had heard of God "by the hearing of the ear", as tradition and the friends spoke of him. Now he has "seen" him in the storm. He had longed for this: "I will see him for myself; my own eyes will see" (19:27). For Jewish and Christian readers alike the verse is a classic statement that knowing God is different from knowing about him. Others read it more darkly: for Curtis, seeing God is what leads Job to reject him (see 42:6); for Greenstein, Job remains defiant. The Testament of Job and many sermons treat it as a vision of grace.

a: That is why I take back what I said
p: The verb has no object. The Plain supplies "what I said" (from 42:3): the retraction reading. Others supply "myself", or read "I melt".
b: Em'as means "I reject, refuse, despise", but the Hebrew gives it no object, so every translation supplies one. Retraction (the Plain): Job rejects what he said, taking the object from 42:3, "So I talked without understanding" (Pope; Habel; the 1985 JPS "recant"; Clines's "I submit" is close). "I despise myself" (repentance): the KJV and most older versions. In Job this verb stands with no stated object when Job's own life is meant: ma'asti in 7:16 ("I give up" on this site) and em'as chayyay in 9:21 ("I reject my life"). The Vulgate has ipse me reprehendo, "I rebuke myself", and the Greek "I despised myself". "I melt away": from a second root, "flow, melt" (compare 7:5, "runs"): the Greek adds "and I melted", and 11QtgJob has "I am poured out and dissolved". Rejection of God: Curtis, "I feel loathing, contempt and revulsion [toward you, O God]". "I am fed up": Greenstein. 11QtgJob is cited from the edition (DJD 23) as reported by Greenstein and van der Lugt; it was not checked directly for this site.

a: I change my mind
t: Nicham 'al: relent about, repent of, be comforted for
p: Nichamti with 'al is a set phrase: "change one's mind about", sometimes "repent of" or "be comforted about".
b: Nichamti (from nacham) followed by 'al is a fixed phrase. Most often it means "change one's mind about, relent concerning": God relents about the harm he had planned (Exodus 32:12, 14; Jeremiah 18:8, 10; Amos 7:3, 6). It can mean "repent of": Jeremiah 8:6 says no one repents of his wickedness, with the same phrase, and this is the strongest support for "I repent". It can also mean "be comforted about" (2 Samuel 13:39, David comforted about Amnon). The traditional "repent in dust and ashes" (KJV; Vulgate ago paenitentiam in favilla et cinere, "I do penance in embers and ashes") takes 'al as "on, in", the place where Job sits (2:8). That is possible but unusual after this verb. The Plain follows the set phrase, "change my mind about". Clines ("accept consolation for") and Greenstein ("take pity on") take the comfort sense.
r: Exodus 32:12; Exodus 32:14; Jeremiah 18:8; Amos 7:3; Jeremiah 8:6; 2 Samuel 13:39; 2:8

a: about dust and ashes
t: Dust and ashes, and the four readings of 42:6
p: "Dust and ashes" elsewhere means human lowliness (30:19; Genesis 18:27). How the phrase is read decides how the book ends.
b: 'Afar va'efer occurs only three times: here; in 30:19, where Job says he is "no better than dust and ashes"; and in Genesis 18:27, where Abraham says, "I am only dust and ashes". Both describe human lowliness. Ashes are also where Job has sat mourning (2:8). The whole verse is read four main ways. Retraction (the Plain): Job withdraws his case and changes his mind about his mourning or his mortal lot (Pope, Patrick, Habel, Morrow; JPS). Repentance: Job repents of rash words, in dust and ashes (Rashi, Calvin, Andersen, Hartley); not of the friends' charges, since God says Job spoke rightly (42:7). Comfort: Job accepts consolation as a mortal (Clines, "I accept consolation for my dust and ashes"; Mitchell; Greenstein, "I take pity on dust and ashes"); Newsom thinks the ambiguity is deliberate. Rejection: Job turns from God and pities humankind (Curtis, "I am sorry for frail man"). The ancient versions lean to lowliness: the Greek ends "I consider myself earth and ashes", 11QtgJob "and I shall become dust and ashes", and the rabbinic Targum, as Mangan translates it, has Job despise his wealth and be consoled over his children, who are dust and ashes.

a: You did not say what is right about me
t: What did Job say that was right?
p: The friends defended God and are condemned; Job accused God and is praised. Every reading of Job must explain why.
b: Nekhonah means what is firm, true or correct. The LORD says it twice (verses 7 and 8). Main views: (1) Job's honesty: he spoke the truth about his experience and kept talking to God, while the friends told lies to protect God (13:7–8). (2) The friends' theology was wrong: suffering is not always punishment (Maimonides reads the friends as representing flawed views of providence). (3) Only Job's last words (40:3–5; 42:1–6) are meant. (4) Elay can mean "to me": Job spoke to God, the friends only about him (Clines discusses this). The Greek reads "you have not spoken anything true before me".
orig: לֹא דִבַּרְתֶּם אֵלַי נְכוֹנָה (lo dibbartem elay nekhonah)

a: my servant Job
p: God calls Job "my servant" four times in verses 7–8, as in 1:8 and 2:3. The test is over and Job passed.
b: In the prologue the LORD twice called Job "my servant" before the Accuser (1:8; 2:3). He does so four times here. The Accuser had bet that Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). He did not. The Accuser himself is never mentioned again; neither is Elihu. Christian readers have compared Job to the suffering servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12, who is also vindicated and intercedes for others.

a: seven bulls and seven rams
p: Seven bulls and seven rams is a royal-sized offering. Balaam asked for the same (Numbers 23:1).
b: Balaam told Balak, "Build me seven altars here, and get ready for me seven bulls and seven rams here" (Numbers 23:1). Seven bulls and seven rams were also offered when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:26) and at Hezekiah's rededication (2 Chronicles 29:21). Job, who once offered burnt offerings for his children (1:5), now serves as a priest for the friends who accused him. The Greek adds, "for if not for him, I would have destroyed you".

a: Job my servant will pray for you
p: God will hear the man the friends said God would not hear. Job prays like Abraham and Moses.
b: God tells Abimelech that Abraham "is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live" (Genesis 20:7). Moses prays for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14), and Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as famous righteous men (Ezekiel 14:14). Eliphaz had promised that if Job repented, God would deliver even the guilty through the cleanness of his hands (22:30). The irony: it is Eliphaz who is saved by Job's prayer. "I will accept him" is literally "I will lift his face", to show favor.

a: the disgrace your folly has earned
t: Nevalah: the friends are the fools
p: Nevalah, "folly, disgrace", echoes 2:10, where Job told his wife she talked like a godless woman (naval).
b: Nevalah comes from the same root as naval, a senseless or godless fool. In the prologue Job told his wife, "You are talking the way a godless woman talks" (2:10, hannevalot). Now God says it is the friends who have earned nevalah. The frame of the book ends by turning the word on the comforters. The clause can also be read "so that I do not do something disgraceful to you", that is, punish them as their folly deserves.

a: the LORD turned Job's fortunes around
p: Shav shevut, literally "turn the captivity", means "restore the fortunes". It is the prophets' phrase for the end of exile.
b: The Hebrew is literally "turned back the captivity of Job", as the KJV has it. Job was never a prisoner, so the Plain gives the meaning, a complete turnaround of his fortunes. But it is the prophets' word for bringing the exiles home: "Then the LORD your God will turn back your captivity and show you compassion" (Deuteronomy 30:3; also Jeremiah 29:14; Psalm 126:4). For readers after the exile, Job's restoration would sound like their own hope. Note the timing: it comes "when Job prayed for his friends", not when he repented.

a: until it was double
p: Under the law a thief found out repays double. Job's double restoration may hint at God settling Job's case.
b: This is my suggestion, not a standard reading. In the law of Exodus, "If the stolen animal... is actually found alive in his hand, he repays two for one" (Exodus 22:4), and in a dispute brought "before God", "The one God finds guilty must repay his neighbor two for one" (Exodus 22:9). Job had framed his complaint as a lawsuit and said God had taken what was his (1:21; 19:6–9). If the poet had this law in mind, the double restoration is God paying as the losing party pays, while never admitting fault. Against this: double portions also mean honor (Deuteronomy 21:17; Isaiah 61:7), which is the simpler reading. I do not know of a published source that presses the legal link this way, so treat it as a possibility.

a: His brothers came, all of them, and all his sisters
p: Job's brothers and sisters show up only now, after the turn. In 19:13–14 they had stayed away.
b: Job had complained, "My brothers he has moved far away from me" (19:13). Now that God has restored him, the family arrives, eats with him and comforts him. Some readers see a touching reunion; others see irony, as the relatives come back with the good times. They "shook their heads with him and comforted him", the very words used of the three friends when they first arrived (2:11), so the book comes full circle.

a: for all the harm the LORD had brought on him
p: The narrator says plainly that the LORD brought the harm. The Accuser is gone from the story.
b: In chapters 1–2 the Accuser struck Job's goods and body, with the LORD's permission (1:12; 2:6–7). Now the narrator says simply that the LORD brought it all. The book does not let God off by blaming a lesser power. Jewish and Christian readers have explained this as God's sovereignty over what he allows; critical scholars note that the prose ending speaks as if the Accuser had never been. Either way, Job's own words ("The LORD gave, and the LORD took", 1:21) are confirmed.

a: one coin
p: A qesitah is an old unit of money, used only here and in the stories of Jacob and Joshua.
b: Qesitah occurs only here, in Genesis 33:19 (Jacob buys land at Shechem for a hundred qesitah) and Joshua 24:32. Its value is unknown. This site's Genesis and Joshua keep the Hebrew word ("qesitahs"); here the Plain says "coin". The Talmud says that in Africa a small coin was still called qesitah (Rosh Hashanah 26a). The Greek and, it seems, the Qumran Targum render it "a lamb". Its use gives the ending an old, patriarchal feel. The gold ring (nezem) is a nose or ear ring, like Rebekah's (Genesis 24:22).

a: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand pairs of oxen and a thousand female donkeys
p: Every number in 1:3 is doubled: 7,000 to 14,000 sheep, 3,000 to 6,000 camels, 500 to 1,000 oxen and donkeys.
b: Compare 1:3: seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred pairs of oxen and five hundred female donkeys. Every figure doubles. But the children do not: Job again has seven sons and three daughters (verse 13). An old sermon point, found for example in Matthew Henry's commentary (1708), is that his first children were not lost but gone before, so they too are doubled. Readers who find the ending too neat point out that new children do not replace dead ones.

a: He came to have seven sons and three daughters
p: The word for "seven" has an odd form, shiv'anah. The Targum and Rashi read it as "twice seven", fourteen sons.
b: Here "seven" is shiv'anah, found nowhere else. It may be an old or dialect form. The rabbinic Targum and Rashi took it as a doubled seven, so that Job's sons, like his flocks, were doubled to fourteen, while the three daughters (who are praised and named) stayed three. Most translations read seven, as in 1:2.

a: Jemimah
p: Jemimah "dove" (or "day"), Keziah "cassia" (a perfume), Keren-happuch "horn of eye-paint".
b: Yemimah probably means "dove" (Arabic yamamah); the Greek took it as "Day" (Hemera), from yom. Qetsi'ah is cassia, a fragrant bark (Psalm 45:8). Qeren-happukh is a "horn of pukh", a cosmetics jar of black eye-paint (Jezebel painted her eyes with pukh, 2 Kings 9:30). The Greek has "Horn of Amaltheia", the horn of plenty of Greek myth. The sons are not named; the daughters are, and their names speak of beauty and pleasure. After a book of ashes and sores, the ending is fragrant.

a: Their father gave them property to inherit side by side with their brothers
p: Under Israel's law daughters inherited only when there were no sons. Job gives his daughters a share alongside their brothers.
b: In Numbers 27, God tells Moses, "Zelophehad's daughters have spoken rightly. Yes, give them land to own as an inheritance among their father's brothers" (Numbers 27:7), and the rule is "When a man dies without a son, hand his inheritance over to his daughter" (Numbers 27:8). Job goes further: his daughters inherit while they have brothers. Some see a sign of Job's new generosity, others a custom outside Israel (Job is from Uz), or a sign of the abundance of his restored house. The Testament of Job (chapters 46–50) retells the scene: the daughters receive heavenly sashes that let them speak in the language of angels.

a: four generations of them
p: A hundred and forty years is twice seventy, the normal span of life (Psalm 90:10).
b: A hundred and forty years is double the seventy years of Psalm 90:10, so even Job's life is doubled, if one assumes he was about seventy when the trials began. Seeing four generations is a blessing (Genesis 50:23; Psalm 128:6). The Greek gives different numbers (see the variant).

a: old and satisfied with days
p: The same words are used of Isaac (Genesis 35:29); Abraham died "old and satisfied" (Genesis 25:8).
b: Isaac "died and was gathered to his people, old and satisfied with days" (Genesis 35:29), and Abraham died "at a good old age, old and satisfied" (Genesis 25:8). David too dies "satisfied with days" (1 Chronicles 29:28). The ending places Job among the patriarchs. Many Jewish and Christian readers have dated him to their time for this reason. The Greek adds a long ending (see the variant).
